A–Z style of art movements with key works and artists.
Classical art (~480 BCE–5th century CE): The art of ancient Greece and Rome, built on idealized proportion, balance and the human body.
Byzantine art (~330–1453): The art of the eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople. Gold mosaics and icons present sacred figures as timeless.
Islamic art (7th century onward): Art of the Islamic world, favoring calligraphy, geometry and arabesque over figures in religious settings.
Romanesque (~1000–1150): Solid stone churches with round arches and carved portals; heavy walls with small windows.
Gothic (~1140–1500): Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses allowed tall, light-filled cathedrals with stained glass.
Renaissance (~1400–1600): A 'rebirth' of classical ideals, linear perspective and close observation of nature.
Baroque (~1600–1750): Drama, movement and strong contrasts of light, used to stir the emotions.
Rococo (~1730–1780): A lighter, ornamental and playful style of pastel colors and curving forms.
Neoclassicism (~1760–1830): A return to the clarity, order and moral seriousness of antiquity, boosted by the discoveries at Pompeii.
Romanticism (~1800–1850): Emotion, imagination and the awe of nature over reason and order.
Realism (~1840s–1880s): Depicting ordinary people and daily life honestly, without idealization. Also used for later works of everyday modern life.
Ukiyo-e (~1650–1900): Japanese woodblock prints of 'the floating world': actors, landscapes, beauties. A major influence on European artists.
Impressionism (~1870–1886): Painting the effect of light and atmosphere with short, visible brushstrokes, often outdoors.
Post-Impressionism (~1885–1905): Artists who built on Impressionism but sought more structure, emotion or symbol.
Fauvism (~1905–1908): Bold, non-naturalistic color. 'Fauves' means wild beasts.
Expressionism (~1905–1930s): Distorting form and color to express inner feeling. Groups such as Die Brücke and Der Blaue Reiter.
Cubism (~1907–1920s): Objects broken into geometric planes and shown from many viewpoints at once.
Suprematism (~1915–1920s): Malevich's art of basic geometric forms, as 'the supremacy of pure feeling'.
De Stijl (1917–1931): Dutch movement reducing art and design to straight lines and primary colors.
Dada (~1916–1924): An anti-art protest born in the First World War; it mocked reason, nationalism and tradition.
Surrealism (~1924–1950s): Exploring dreams, the unconscious and chance. Artists like Dalí, Magritte, Ernst and Kahlo.
Modernist architecture (~1900–1970): Function, new materials and clear forms replaced historical ornament.
Abstract Expressionism (~1940s–1960): Large abstract canvases that express emotion through gesture or fields of color. Pollock, Rothko, de Kooning.
Pop Art (~1950s–1970s): Borrowing from advertising, comics and mass media, using irony and repetition.
Minimalism (~1960s–1970s): Stripped-down geometric forms and industrial materials. Associated with Donald Judd and Agnes Martin. Kusama's early work is often discussed alongside it.
Conceptual art (~1960s onward): The idea is more important than the finished object. Includes text pieces, performance and installations.
Street art and graffiti (~1970s onward): Art made in public space without permission, or in dialogue with it, from tags and murals to stencils.
Digital art (~1960s onward): Art made with or about computers: algorithmic, networked, generative and interactive work.
Profiles of artists across art history.

Phidias (c. 480–430 BCE), Greek sculptor: The leading sculptor of Classical Athens, said to have supervised the Parthenon sculptures and made the lost gold-and-ivory statues of Athena and Zeus. None of his works survive in original form.
Thutmose (active c. 1350 BCE), Egyptian sculptor: Court sculptor under Akhenaten at Amarna. His workshop yielded the famed bust of Nefertiti.
Myron (active c. 480–440 BCE), Greek sculptor: Known for lifelike athletes in bronze, especially the Discobolus. His works survive only in Roman copies.
Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337), Italian painter: Broke from the flat Byzantine tradition by painting solid figures with human emotion.
Jan van Eyck (c. 1390–1441), Netherlandish painter: A pioneer of oil painting, noted for jewel-like detail and light.
Sandro Botticelli (c. 1445–1510), Italian painter: Florentine painter of graceful lines. Worked for the Medici family.

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), Italian painter, scientist: A painter, engineer and anatomist who filled thousands of notebook pages with drawings and ideas. Fewer than 20 paintings are attributed to him.
Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), German printmaker, painter: Raised the status of printmaking and made some of the first self-portraits in Northern art.
Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564), Italian sculptor, painter, architect: Carved the David and the Pietà, painted the Sistine ceiling, and designed the dome of St Peter's.
Raphael (1483–1520), Italian painter, architect: Famous for harmonious compositions and gentle Madonnas. He died at 37.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder (c. 1525–1569), Flemish painter: Painted peasant life, proverbs and winter landscapes with humor and moral bite.
Caravaggio (1571–1610), Italian painter: Used harsh light and ordinary models for sacred scenes. He had a violent life and spent his last years fleeing a murder charge.
Artemisia Gentileschi (1593–c. 1656), Italian painter: One of the most successful women artists of her time and the first woman admitted to Florence's art academy.
Gian Lorenzo Bernini (1598–1680), Italian sculptor, architect: The dominant figure of Roman Baroque, designing St Peter's piazza and carving dramatic marble figures.
Diego Velázquez (1599–1660), Spanish painter: Court painter to Philip IV of Spain. Admired by later painters for his loose brushwork.
Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669), Dutch painter, printmaker: Master of light and psychological depth; made nearly 100 self-portraits over his career.
Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675), Dutch painter: Painted quiet interiors lit by window light. About 35 paintings are attributed to him.
Jean-Honoré Fragonard (1732–1806), French painter: Painted playful, romantic scenes for aristocratic patrons.
Francisco Goya (1746–1828), Spanish painter, printmaker: Court painter who also recorded war and human cruelty, and later made haunting 'Black Paintings'.
Jacques-Louis David (1748–1825), French painter: The leading painter of the French Revolution and later of Napoleon.
Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849), Japanese printmaker, painter: Produced thousands of designs over 70 years. The Great Wave is his most famous.
J. M. W. Turner (1775–1851), English painter: Painted light and atmosphere, moving toward near-abstraction in his later work.
Eugène Delacroix (1798–1863), French painter: Leader of French Romanticism, favoring color and emotion over line.
Gustave Courbet (1819–1877), French painter: Insisted on painting 'what I see', including working people.
Édouard Manet (1832–1883), French painter: A bridge between realism and Impressionism, famous for bold, flat handling.
Gustave Eiffel (1832–1923), French engineer: Built bridges, viaducts and the Eiffel Tower with his firm; also worked on the structure of the Statue of Liberty.
Paul Cézanne (1839–1906), French painter: Rebuilt painting out of geometric structure, and was called the father of modern art by Picasso and Matisse.
Claude Monet (1840–1926), French painter: Painted the same subjects in different light, such as haystacks, cathedrals and water lilies.
Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890), Dutch painter: Made about 2,000 artworks in roughly a decade. Sold very little in his lifetime.
Georges Seurat (1859–1891), French painter: Developed pointillism and died at 31.
Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959), American architect: Advocated 'organic architecture' in harmony with its setting.
Henri Matisse (1869–1954), French painter: Used bold color and simple shapes; late in life he made cut-paper works.
Piet Mondrian (1872–1944), Dutch painter: Reduced painting to straight lines and primary colors.
Wassily Kandinsky (1866–1944), Russian painter: Often credited with painting one of the first fully abstract works.
Kazimir Malevich (1879–1935), Russian painter: Founded Suprematism, centered on pure geometric forms.
Pablo Picasso (1881–1973), Spanish painter, sculptor: Co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque and changed style many times across a very long career.
Edward Hopper (1882–1967), American painter: Painted quiet scenes of American city and small-town life.
Marcel Duchamp (1887–1968), French-American artist: Introduced the 'ready-made' and shifted the idea of art from craft to concept.
Salvador Dalí (1904–1989), Spanish painter: Meticulous dreamlike painting and a talent for self-promotion.
Frida Kahlo (1907–1954), Mexican painter: Painted about 55 self-portraits, drawing on her pain, identity and Mexican culture.
Louise Bourgeois (1911–2010), French-American sculptor: Her sculpture and installations explore memory, family and the body, and she achieved wide fame in her 70s.
Jackson Pollock (1912–1956), American painter: Known for 'drip' paintings made by moving around canvases laid on the floor.
Andy Warhol (1928–1987), American artist: Turned celebrity and consumer goods into art using silkscreen printing.
Yayoi Kusama (b. 1929), Japanese artist: Famous for polka dots, infinity rooms and pumpkins. Her work draws on hallucinations she has experienced since childhood.
Frank Gehry (b. 1929), Canadian-American architect: Known for sculptural, flowing buildings such as the Guggenheim Bilbao.
Ai Weiwei (b. 1957), Chinese artist, activist: Uses installation, film and social media to comment on politics and human rights.
Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960–1988), American painter: Began as a graffiti artist, then painted dense, text-filled canvases about race, power and class. He died at 27.
Damien Hirst (b. 1965), English artist: Leader of the Young British Artists, known for animals in formaldehyde.
Banksy (anonymous), British street artist: An anonymous artist whose stenciled works appear on city walls and in the art market.
Beeple (Mike Winkelmann) (b. 1981), American digital artist: Made one digital image every day since 2007. His 2021 sale put digital art in the spotlight.
Fan Kuan (c. 960–1030), Chinese painter: A Song-dynasty landscape painter, known for monumental mountain scenes. Travelers Among Mountains and Streams is the work most firmly attributed to him.

t: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
d: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, Georges Seurat, 1884–86. Thousands of tiny dots of color (pointillism) form a leisurely park scene, built from scientific ideas about color.
The Starry Night, Vincent van Gogh, 1889. Painted from memory of the view from his window at the asylum at Saint-Rémy, with swirling sky and a cypress. A study in
The Basket of Apples, Paul Cézanne, c. 1893. Table and objects are seen from several viewpoints at once. This prepared the ground for Cubism.
Eiffel Tower, Gustave Eiffel's company, 1887–89. Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it was criticized by some artists at first. It is now a symbol of iron-age engineering
The Dance (II), Henri Matisse, 1910. Five nude figures dance in a ring, painted in three flat colors: red, blue and green. A radical simplification.
Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Pablo Picasso, 1907. Five women in angular, mask-like forms break with perspective. Often called the starting point of Cubism.

The Persistence of Memory, Salvador Dalí, 1931. Soft melting watches drape over a dreamlike landscape. Small in size, enormous in fame.
Fallingwater, Frank Lloyd Wright, 1935–37. A house cantilevered over a waterfall, built to blend with nature while using modern materials.
Guernica, Pablo Picasso, 1937. A monochrome mural responding to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. It became a universal image
The Two Fridas, Frida Kahlo, 1939. Two versions of the artist sit side by side, hearts exposed and joined by a vein. Painted around the time of her divorce
Nighthawks, Edward Hopper, 1942. Four people in an all-night diner seen through a glass wall. A portrait of urban loneliness.
Broadway Boogie Woogie, Piet Mondrian, 1942–43. A grid of colored squares inspired by New York streets and jazz, breaking Mondrian's earlier strict black lines.
Autumn Rhythm (Number 30), Jackson Pollock, 1950. Paint dripped and poured onto a canvas laid on the floor. The act of painting becomes visible.
Campbell's Soup Cans, Andy Warhol, 1962. Thirty-two canvases, one for each soup flavor then sold. Mass-produced goods are treated as fine art.

Cross-era essays that follow one idea through art history.
Much of the world's art was made to honor gods or to guide worship.
Rulers have used art to proclaim authority, and artists have used it to question authority.
Nature has been a subject, a source of materials and a mirror of feeling.
From fertility figures to athletes and self-portraits, artists keep returning to the body.
New tools change what art looks like: oil paint, the printing press, photography, and now software.
How art is made: materials, tools and methods.
Pigments are colored powders mixed with a binder. Early artists used ochre, charcoal and manganese. Later came lapis lazuli blue, vermilion, lead whit
Water-based pigment applied to wet plaster, so the color becomes part of the wall. Buon fresco demands speed: only the area that can be painted in a d
Pigment ground in drying oil such as linseed. Oil dries slowly, so it can be blended and built up in glazes. It spread from Northern Europe in the 15t
Metal poured into a mold. Lost-wax casting, used from ancient Greece to Ife and Benin, allows very fine detail.
Sculptors remove material, revealing a form. Marble is prized for its translucence. Michelangelo spoke of freeing a figure from the block.
Images printed from a prepared surface: woodcut, engraving, etching, lithography. Multiples let art circulate widely and cheaply.
Colored glass pieces held in lead strips. In Gothic cathedrals it fills walls with changing light and tells Bible stories to those who could not read.
Materials and structural ideas shape buildings: the arch and dome in Rome, the flying buttress in Gothic Europe, iron in the 19th century, reinforced
Software, video, mirrors, light and found objects. The ready-made and the installation expanded what materials count as art.
